passages.happening:
“But now they mock me, men younger than I am, whose fathers I would have refused to entrust with my sheep dogs” (verse 1). They were men driven out by hunger, gnawing the dry land and eating mallow and the roots of the broom tree, shouted out of town like thieves, living in holes among the rocks.

“And now they mock me in song; I have become a byword among them. They abhor me and keep far from me; they do not hesitate to spit in my face” (verses 9-10). Because God has unstrung his bow, they throw off all restraint. They come at him like an army through a wide breach in a wall. ‘Terrors are turned loose against me; they drive away my dignity as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed like a cloud’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is the second part of Job's final speech. Chapter 29 remembered the months gone by. The word now, attah, opens this chapter and returns in verses 9 and 16, marking each stage of his fall. Chapter 29 ended with Job like a king among his troops. Chapter 30 begins with him mocked by the lowest members of society.

The men he describes were outcasts who lived on the desert fringe, scavenging among the shrubs and sheltering in holes in the sides of dry riverbeds. Their lives were desperate. Dogs in that world were mostly scavengers and working animals, not pets, so verse 1 is a sharp insult.

Spitting in someone's face was among the gravest insults there was, and a byword was a name turned into a proverb of disaster. The siege pictures of verses 12 to 14 come from ancient warfare.
passages.later: The broom tree was desert shrub, the one Elijah lay down under in despair: ‘He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die’ (1 Kings 19:4).
passages.hard:
How can Job, who defended the poor, speak with such contempt about the outcasts in verses 1 to 8?

Many readers are troubled by this. Job calls the men who mock him a senseless and nameless brood, whose fathers were not fit to be trusted with his dogs. It seems at odds with the Job of chapter 29, who was a father to the needy.

Some interpreters say it shows a real flaw in Job: his kindness flowed downward from a place of honor, and he never regarded the very lowest as his equals. The later chapters, in which God humbles Job, may speak to this. Others read the section as the bitterness of a man in extreme pain, not his settled view. His point is not to despise the poor but to show how far he has fallen, that even the lowest now look down on him. A third reading notes that these are not simply the poor but men who have joined in mocking a sufferer.

The readings can be held together. The book does not ask the reader to approve every word Job says in his pain, and it records this passage honestly.
passages.asks: Job's honor had been real, and so was his contempt for those beneath him. Ask whether there is anyone you look down on, even while you help them. And ask how you would want to be spoken of if you fell to where they are.

passages.happening:
“And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction grip me. Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest” (verses 16-17). God has seized him by the collar of his tunic. ‘He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes’ (verse 19).

“I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me. You have ruthlessly turned on me; You oppose me with Your strong hand” (verses 20-21). God snatches him up into the wind and tosses him in the storm. ‘Yes, I know that You will bring me down to death, to the place appointed for all the living’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Job now speaks to God directly, as You, and accuses him of cruelty. His description of his body matches the disease of the prologue: pain that gnaws at night, and later in the chapter skin that blackens and peels and bones that burn with fever.

Dust and ashes is a rhyming pair in Hebrew, afar va'efer. Job will use it again, at the very end, when he speaks to God after the whirlwind (42:6).

His cry in verse 20 is one of the hardest in the book. He calls out, and God only looks at him. The Bible records it as it was spoken.
passages.later: Abraham used the same words of himself before God: ‘though I am but dust and ashes’ (Genesis 18:27).
passages.asks: Job cried out and heard nothing back. Ask whether you have prayed into silence. And ask what kept you praying, or what might.

passages.happening:
“Yet no one stretches out his hand to a ruined man when he cries for help in his distress. Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?” (verses 24-25).

“But when I hoped for good, evil came; when I looked for light, darkness fell” (verse 26). He churns inside and cannot rest. He goes about blackened, but not by the sun, and stands up in the assembly crying for help. ‘I have become a brother of jackals, a companion of ostriches’ (verse 29). His skin grows black and peels, and his bones burn with fever.

“My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Job once wept for others in trouble. Now no one reaches out a hand to him. The word for affliction, oni, is related to the word for the afflicted poor whom Job once protected. He has become one of them.

Jackals and ostriches were desert creatures known for their mournful cries at night. To be their brother was to share their lonely lament.

The harp and flute, once used for joy, now play only mourning. It is a reversal of the celebrations Job described in 21:12, where the wicked danced to the lyre and the flute.
passages.later: The prophet Micah mourns with the same creatures: “I will howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich” (Micah 1:8).
passages.asks: No one stretched out a hand to Job. Ask who in your church or town has cried for help and been left alone. And ask what it would take for you to be the one who reaches out.
